facts.statement: Paralititan was described by American paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues in 2001.
facts.quote: It was described by American paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues in 2001.

facts.statement: Fossils of Paralititan were found by an American expedition in the Bahariya Oasis, western Egypt.
facts.quote: These fossils were unearthed by an American expedition to the Bahariya Oasis in western Egypt in rock layers of the Bahariya Formation.

facts.statement: An incomplete dorsal vertebra described by Ernst Stromer in 1932 was later assigned to Paralititan.
facts.quote: An incomplete dorsal (back) vertebra that had been described by German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in 1932 was also assigned to Paralititan.

facts.statement: Researcher Joshua Smith rediscovered the fossil site Gebel el Dist in 1999, where Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf had worked between 1912 and 1914.
facts.quote: In 1999, researcher Joshua Smith rediscovered a site in the Bahariya Oasis of Egypt, known as Gebel el Dist, that had formerly been explored by Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf between 1912 and 1914.

facts.statement: A partial sauropod skeleton was found at the nearby site of Gebel Fagga during an expedition.
facts.quote: At a new site, the nearby Gebel Fagga, the expedition succeeded in locating a partial sauropod skeleton.

facts.statement: In 2001, an international team led by Joshua B. Smith described the partial skeleton as the new species Paralititan stromeri.
facts.quote: In 2001, an international crew made up of paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues described the partial skeleton as a new genus and species of sauropod dinosaur, named Paralititan stromeri.

facts.statement: The specific name 'stromeri' honors Ernst Stromer, who first found dinosaur fossils in the Bahariya Oasis in 1911.
facts.quote: The specific name is in honor of Stromer, who first established the presence of dinosaur fossils in the Bahariya Oasis during a 1911 expedition.

facts.statement: A large anterior dorsal vertebra assigned to Paralititan by Stromer in 1932 was destroyed during the Bombing of Munich in World War II.
facts.quote: Stromer, in 1932, assumed that this vertebra belonged to an undetermined "Giant Sauropod", but it was destroyed alongside other fossils from the Bahariya Formation during the Bombing of Munich in World War II.

facts.statement: Paralititan lived in present-day Egypt during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Paralititan (meaning "tidal giant") is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day Egypt during the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The Bahariya Formation where Paralititan fossils were found dates to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: This formation dates to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, which lasted .

facts.statement: Paralititan had a robust humerus measuring 1.69 meters in length with a large deltopectoral crest.
facts.quote: Its robust humerus (upper arm bone) is 1.69 m in length and bears a large deltopectoral crest (a forward directed bony flange).

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Paralititan were wider than tall and lacked pleurocoels.
facts.quote: The caudal (tail) vertebrae are wider than tall and lack pleurocoels (large cavities that stored air sacs) on their sides.

facts.statement: Paralititan is classified as a member of the family Saltasauridae within the superfamily Titanosauria.
facts.quote: Paralititan is a member of the Saltasauridae, a family within the sauropod group Titanosauria.

facts.statement: Recent estimates suggest Paralititan was about 26 meters long and weighed between 30 and 55 tonnes.
facts.quote: More recent estimates place it at 26 m in length and 30–55 tonnes (33.1–60.6 short tons) in mass.

facts.statement: Paralititan coexisted with dinosaurs including the sauropod Aegyptosaurus and theropods such as Tameryraptor, Spinosaurus, and Bahariasaurus.
facts.quote: Paralititan coexisted with other dinosaurs such as the sauropod Aegyptosaurus, the theropods Tameryraptor, Spinosaurus, and Bahariasaurus, and an unnamed abelisaurid theropod.

facts.statement: During the Cenomanian, the Bahariya Formation was located on the margin of the Tethys Sea and consisted of mangrove swamps, rivers, and tidal flats.
facts.quote: During the Cenomanian, the Bahariya Formation was on the margin of the Tethys Sea, and represented a large network of mangrove swamps, rivers, and tidal flats.

facts.statement: It is debated whether several isolated sauropod fossils previously assigned to Aegyptosaurus actually belong to Paralititan.
facts.quote: Several isolated sauropod fossils, mainly consisting of caudal vertebrae, were assigned by Stromer to the other Bahariya sauropod Aegyptosaurus, but these may belong to Paralititan instead.

facts.statement: Only 5.1% of Paralititan's skeleton is known, making exact size estimates difficult.
facts.quote: Only 5.1% of Paralititan's skeleton is known, so its exact size is difficult to estimate.

facts.statement: American paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter estimated Paralititan's length at around 26 meters in a 2006 study.
facts.quote: Using Saltasaurus as a guide, American paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter estimated its length at around 26 m in a 2006 study.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Paralititan's length at over 20 meters and weight at 20 tonnes in his 2010 book.
facts.quote: In the 2010 edition of his book The Princeton Field Guide to Dinosaurs, American researcher Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 20+ meters (66+ ft), and its weight at 20 tonnes (24.2 short tons).

facts.statement: Bernardo González Riga and colleagues estimated Paralititan's weight at approximately 50 metric tonnes in 2016.
facts.quote: In 2016, using equations that estimate body mass based on the circumference of the humerus and femur of quadrupedal animals, Argentine paleontologist Bernardo González Riga and colleagues gave a weight estimate of ~50 MT for Paralititan.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Paralititan's weight between 30 and 55 tonnes in 2019.
facts.quote: In 2019, Paul estimated Paralititan between 30 and 55 tonnes (33.1–60.6 short tons) in weight.

facts.statement: Paralititan sacral vertebrae lack pleurocoels, which are large air-filled spaces found in other titanosaurs.
facts.quote: The sacral vertebrae of Paralititan lack pleurocoels, large spaces in the sides of the vertebra that stored pneumatic air sacs.

facts.statement: One proximal caudal vertebra of Paralititan has a centrum that is wider than tall and features a convex rear articular condyle.
facts.quote: One of the proximal (towards body) caudal vertebrae has a wider than tall, procoelous centrum with a convex rear articular condyle.

facts.statement: The scapula of Paralititan possesses a medial concavity bordered by a prominent rugosity, a feature shared with other titanosaurs.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) has a medial (inner) concavity that is bordered by a prominent rugosity, like in the titanosaurs Aeolosaurus, Lirainosaurus, Neuquensaurus, and Saltasaurus.

facts.statement: The humerus of Paralititan measures 1.69 meters in length and has greatly expanded upper and lower ends.
facts.quote: Paralititan's humerus is huge at 1.69 m in length, with greatly expanded upper and lower ends.

facts.statement: The deltopectoral crest on the Paralititan humerus stretches for more than 53% of the bone's total length.
facts.quote: The deltopectoral crest is large, stretching for more than 53% of the length of the humerus.

facts.statement: The known Paralititan metacarpal has a rectangular, flattened surface indicating the reduction or absence of phalanges on that digit.
facts.quote: The metacarpal known from Paralititan has a rectangular, flattened surface indicative phalangeal reduction or absence on this digit.

facts.statement: Paralititan differs from Aegyptosaurus by being larger, possibly lacking pleurocoels in its front tail vertebrae, and having a relatively longer deltopectoral crest.
facts.quote: Paralititan differs from Aegyptosaurus in its larger size, possibly in not having pleurocoels in its front tail vertebrae, and in possessing a relatively longer deltopectoral crest on its humerus.

facts.statement: Paralititan belongs to the Lithostrotia group, which existed during the Cretaceous period on all continents except Australia.
facts.quote: Paralititan belonged to the group Lithostrotia, a group of sauropods that existed during the Cretaceous period in every continent except for Australia.

facts.statement: Paralititan is classified as a member of the subfamily Saltasaurinae, specifically within an Afro-European clade alongside Abditosaurus.
facts.quote: Based on the study, Paralititan was a member of Saltasaurinae, a subfamily that is divided in two clades: Saltasaurini, endemic to South America, and an Afro-European clade formed by Paralititan and Abditosaurus.

facts.statement: Paralititan is the first dinosaur confirmed to have inhabited a mangrove habitat.
facts.quote: Paralititan is the first dinosaur demonstrated to have inhabited a mangrove habitat.

facts.statement: The environment where Paralititan lived was a mangrove-dominated coastal area bordering the Tethys Sea, characterized by vast tidal flats and waterways.
facts.quote: This mangrove system bordered the Tethys Sea, which transformed the region into a mangrove-dominated coastal environment filled with vast tidal flats and waterways.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Paralititan was preserved in autochthonous tidal flat deposits containing mangrove vegetation and root marks.
facts.quote: The autochthonous (a fossil deposit with remains that were not moved by biological or physical processes), associated holotype skeleton was preserved in tidal flat deposits with a mangrove vegetation of seed ferns, Weichselia reticulata, according to the occurrence of plant fossils and root marks in the sediments.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the presence of a large Carcharodontosaurus tooth near the Paralititan skeleton indicates the sauropod was scavenged by the carnivore.
facts.quote: Smith and colleagues (2001) stated that this is evidence of the holotype being scavenged by a carnivorous dinosaur as the tooth is larger than the clasts that could be transported in the tidal flat channels, indicating that the Carcharodontosaurus individual moved towards the site and shed its tooth there.

facts.statement: Smith and colleagues (2001) originally classified Paralititan within the now-unused clade Titanosauridae.
facts.quote: Smith and colleagues (2001) considered Paralititan a member of Titanosauridae, a now unused clade name, alongside Saltasaurus, Malawisaurus, Opisthocoelicaudia, Epachthosaurus, and Alamosaurus.

facts.statement: Many later studies did not determine the phylogenetic placement of Paralititan, likely due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil record.
facts.quote: However, many later studies did not analyze the phylogenetic placement of Paralititan, likely on account of its fragmentary nature.

facts.statement: Studies by Kristina Curry Rogers (2005) and Philip D. Mannion and Paul Upchurch (2011) recovered Paralititan as a basal titanosaurian.
facts.quote: In studies by American paleontologist Kristina Curry Rogers (2005) and British paleontologists Philip D. Mannion and Paul Upchurch (2011), Paralititan was recovered as a basal titanosaurian in their phylogenetic analyses.
